newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA TO PAY OVER $130 MLN BRADY COUPON FRIDAY.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA TO PAY OVER $130 MLN BRADY COUPON FRIDAY.

text.p: Bulgaria will pay around $130 million coupon on its Brady bonds on Friday, Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) governor said on Wednesday.
"The central bank will transfer over $130 million coupon payment on Brady bonds (to the debt agent) on July 25," Svetoslav Gavriiski told Reuters.

Bulgaria issued on July 28, 1994 three types of Brady bonds with a total par of $5.1 billion as part of a restructuring deal on its $8.16 billion commercial debt to the so-called London Club of creditor banks.
Interest on the bonds is due on January 28 and July 28 each year. Transfers are made by the BNB to the debt agent Citibank of Citicorp, which distributes the payment to investors.

Last week Gavriiski said the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was expected this week to evaluate Bulgaria's reform progress under a $657 million funding package before deciding whether to disburse the second tranche of 100 million of Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) or around $137 million.

In April the IMF disbursed $178.7 million of the package, including the $31.704 million worth first tranche of a 14-month $510 million standby credit and $147.043 million of Compensatory and Contingency Financing Facility for grain imports.

The IMF approved the standby in April to enable Bulgaria to carry out delayed reforms by introduction of a currency board system, a restrictive fixed exchange rate mechanism designed to curb inflation and stabilise the local lev currency.
Bulgarian Brady bond prices hit record highs this month after the country introduced the system on July 1 and pegged the lev to the mark as anchor currency at an exchange rate of 1,000.
Bulgarian debt prices were up between 27 and 40 percent for the three respective types of paper on July 22 compared to the beginning of April on the international sovereign debt market.

A new parliament that was elected in early general election in April amended banking legislation to instil stricter financial discipline and approved a restrictive 1997 budget to make currency board operational.
A new reformist government that took office in May has moved towards closing state loss-makers and speeding up privatisation to support balance of payments and budget spending.
Under the currency board the central bank is banned from lending to commercial banks and the government. -- Sofia Newsroom, (++359-2) 911 88
